analysis.title: "Two Premia Down, One To Go": Goldman Says The Global Bond Rout Is Exhausted, But Yields Haven't Peaked
key_insights: Goldman's Vitali Meschoulam argues the Democratic midterm sweep moderated two forces that pushed markets to extremes: the AI infrastructure premium in equities and the Iran risk premium in oil and inflation.

With 10y real yields at roughly 2.50%-2.60%, Goldman says the market 'remains on the constraint side of the framework'. The year-end call is exhaustion of the sell-off, not yet a secular duration rally.
The 2026 bond rout was a real-yield story. Inflation swaps barely moved while nominal 10Y and real yields climbed together.

Since Oct 30 the Philly semis (SOX) are down 12.1% and S&P Energy is down 11.9%, versus the S&P 500 down 2.7%. Staples and Financials are higher. Goldman reads the drawdown as political and sector-specific rather than macro.

Goldman says the AI theme is 'being repriced, not invalidated'. Cash-generative hyperscalers can sustain investment. Marginal infrastructure projects must clear a much higher real hurdle rate. Companies capturing AI productivity gains without financing the buildout may offer cleaner upside.

Goldman calls the equity correction 'the first test of the transmission thesis'. If employment, consumption, lending and non-AI capex hold, it is political and sector repricing. If earnings weakness broadens, spreads widen and hiring slows, the constraint is transmitting to the wider economy.

Since early November 10Y yields are down about 7bp in the US, 15bp in the UK, 7bp in Germany, 10bp in Japan, 13bp in Australia and 14bp in Canada. This extends a 30-45bp retracement that Goldman says 'points to stabilisation, but not (yet) a peak'.

Goldman lists four conditions for the yield pause to hold: de-escalation in oil persists, AI capex actually moderates, lower inflation comes with slower nominal demand, and investors absorb sovereign and long-duration corporate supply without a higher term premium.

Nominal growth is the hinge. If cheap oil lowers inflation while lifting real incomes and margins, the composition of yields changes but their level may not. If nominal growth slows meaningfully, real yields become restrictive and duration rallies. If it falls abruptly, bonds win but spreads widen, stocks fall and the dollar regains a safe-haven bid.

Positioning: Goldman prefers policy-sensitive intermediate maturities that can perform once markets stop adding hikes, over long ends constrained by sovereign issuance, refinancing needs and a higher term premium. With US 2Y yields above 4.5%, investors need more compensation to absorb long-dated supply.

Over the past 12 months the 2Y and 5Y are up 96bp and 97bp versus 56bp for the 30Y. All four tenors are 40-45bp off their highs. The OIS-implied Fed path shifted lower between Oct 30 and Nov 6, with terminal pricing down roughly 10bp (ZeroHedge's read of the chart), and the market still prices hikes.

Goldman's screen shows the US pricing +46bp of tightening over 12 months, the UK +71bp and the euro area +53bp. France's 10Y yield is up 132bp over the year. Japan 10Y is up 96bp with real yields of 0.66%, and Goldman stays out of the Japan duration trade because its policy cycle is still normalising.

Appendix views: prefer the belly to the long end in the US and policy-sensitive core duration in Europe, treat the UK as a conditional convexity trade needing wage and services inflation confirmation, and in EM favor disinflation stories with restrictive real rates (Poland, South Africa, Mexico). Brazil, Turkey and Hungary are carry markets.

Goldman's year-end trade list: selectively buy tech where valuations have reset, favor AI productivity monetizers over marginal infrastructure and financing-dependent names, add intermediate duration, favor EM local rates in credible disinflation stories, and reinstate a moderately weaker-dollar bias.

Goldman's principal risk is that markets confuse the removal of one inflationary tail with the disappearance of structural capital demand. Lower oil can reduce breakevens while real yields stay elevated if sovereign and AI-related corporate issuance remain strong.

ZeroHedge's own view: the shocks are not gone. Brent rebounded 4% the day after its ~9% Nov 4 drop, the US deficit is still about 6% of GDP, and hyperscaler bond issuance has reached $296 billion this year versus Goldman's own $250 billion forecast. ZeroHedge sees the composition of yields changing while the level does not, and points to levered AI borrowers as most exposed.

Renewed conflict restores the oil inflation premium.
AI capex does not moderate and the correction is only a valuation reset.
Lower inflation comes with cheap oil lifting real activity and margins, so yield levels stay high.
Investors demand a higher term premium to absorb sovereign issuance and long-duration corporate debt.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman says the AI theme is repriced, not invalidated. Cash-generative hyperscalers can sustain investment, and AI productivity monetizers offer cleaner upside.
tension_points.bear_case: ZeroHedge argues hyperscaler bond issuance of $296 billion is above Goldman's $250 billion forecast, and a 2.5% real yield is a bigger problem for levered neoclouds than for Microsoft.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Earnings weakness broadens, credit spreads widen and hiring slows, meaning the constraint is transmitting to the wider economy.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman says the sell-off is exhausted. Yields are down 7-15bp across major markets since early November and the odds of more tightening have dipped.

tension_points.what_invalidates: Renewed Iran conflict restoring the oil inflation premium, or investors demanding a higher term premium to absorb sovereign and long-duration corporate supply.
